title: Why You Should Talk Before You Write
author: Naquin, Rod
summary: Prompted by the mixed reception to his own Free Press editorial on AI in the classroom, this piece uses Plato's Phaedrus and the book-burning scene from Don Quixote to make an argument about the structural limits of written communication versus live conversation. Socrates's objection to writing — that a text 'always gives one unvarying answer' and cannot be interrupted or asked to clarify — is paired with the Quixote scene, where a priest and barber judge Quixote's library book by book, with verdicts genuinely argued and reversed in real time, until 'the priest got tired' and the rest burn unread by default rather than by real judgment. The author connects both to his own experience: readers argued with a headline he didn't choose and couldn't defend in the moment, because a published piece 'doesn't take questions.' His central claim is that interruption isn't a flaw in live conversation — it is the entire mechanism by which speech can adjust to the actual person in front of you, something no text, however well-crafted, can ever do. The practical upshot he offers is a genuine self-check for anyone in a leadership or teaching role: before drafting the long email or the reply-all, ask who it's actually for, and whether you could just go ask them directly instead.
points: Uses Socrates's critique in the Phaedrus — that a text 'always gives one unvarying answer' and cannot be questioned — to argue writing structurally cannot adjust to its reader the way conversation can.
Draws a sharp parallel from Don Quixote's book-burning scene: judgments on books were argued and reversed in real time until 'the priest got tired,' and the rest burned by default, not real verdict.
Uses his own experience of a misread Free Press headline to show what it costs to have no way to respond to a reader's question once a piece is published.
Offers a concrete practical move: before drafting the long email or memo, ask who it's actually for, and consider just going to talk to them instead.
quotes: Writing is unfortunately like painting; for the creations of the painter have the attitude of life, and yet if you ask them a question they preserve a solemn silence... if you want to know anything and put a question to one of them, the speaker always gives one unvarying answer.
There was nothing I could say to either group, because a published piece doesn't take questions. I wasn't in the room. The text was.
Nobody won an argument for burning them. The conversation simply cost more than the two men had left to spend, and when the energy ran out, the verdict won by default.

Only a live conversation adjusts to the person in front of you — and it can only adjust because that person can stop you mid-sentence. The interruption isn't noise in the system. The interruption is the system.
Talk is upstream of text. I've said that here about how students learn to write; it turns out it's also true about how adults argue over AI in schools.
